Mr. Speaker, I should like to address two related questions to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The questions are, will the price rebates for export flour announced over the week end place Canadian millers in a position to compete with United States millers, and to what extent does this move mean the institution of a two-price system for wheat and flour in Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to these questions I might give the house some of the background that led up to the new policy with respect to flour which was decided upon by the Canadian wheat board and announced on March 1.
First of all, I should state that exports of wheat from Canada in the form of flour amount to about 40 million bushels per year. It is a considerable item in our wheat trade. The flour trade falls into two main categories. In the first place, the flour goes to some countries which also import wheat, and in

markets of this kind flour exports tend to establish quality standards and have a bearing on the amount of Canadian wheat which can be sold. In addition, however, there are a large number of markets, especially in tropical and semi-tropical countries, where there is no milling industry and the entire breadstuffs market is based upon the importation of flour.
For some time now the wheat board has been carefully watching the flour export position as the market has become increasingly competitive. The most severe competition comes from the United States and from Australia. In both these countries certain advantages are given to flour exports as compared with the export of wheat. This preferred treatment has become an increasingly important competitive factor.
It is this situation that the wheat board feels it must meet. Consequently, effective at 1.15 p.m., March 1, the wheat board announced that, for competitive reasons, it would adjust the position as between export wheat and export flour destined for particular markets. According to the wheat board the adjustment rates on export flour will be announced each day at 3 p.m., Winnipeg time. The adjustment may vary from day to day and also may vary in accordance with the different routes used in exporting Canadian flour. The export flour adjustment which was announced at 3 p.m. Winnipeg time Friday last was as follows: Via Canadian Atlantic or United States Atlantic ports, 4i cents per bushel; via St. Lawrence and Churchill, 3 cents per bushel, and via Canadian Pacific or United States Pacific coast ports 8 cents per bushel.
I should say that the new policy will apply to countries which import mainly flour. The policy will not apply on flour shipments to the United Kingdom, to Europe or to the United States or any United States territories or possessions. The policy announced by the wheat board is definitely a break with tradition. It has been reluctantly adopted by the board because of similar practices in other countries. The wheat board reserves the right to cancel its export flour adjustment policy at any time without notice.

I wonder whether the
minister would now answer the two questions I asked. He has made a statement which is similar to the one released over the week end but he has not answered the two questions I posed with respect to whether these price rebates will put Canadian millers in a position that they can compete with United States millers and, second, to what extent does this move mean the institution of a two-price system fop wheat and flour in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will take those questions as notice. The explanatory memorandum I have given to the house I think contains the answers. But if they are not contained in it, we will see about the matter.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Does the announcement made by the parliamentary assistant that the rebate from the wheat board of 4J- cents to 8 cents for export flour on shipments to certain countries mean that the Canadian farmers are once more being asked to subsidize the millers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production

Mr. Speaker, in order to clear the matter up may I ask this question? Do the Canadian farmers absorb the costs of the rebate made to the millers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question will have to be taken as notice.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the district court at Edmonton has disposed of the case of the Hobbema Indians, would the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration now make a statement to the house on the much-discussed Indian Act of 1951 and suggested amendments thereto.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will do so with the greatest possible satisfaction. It has not been particularly pleasant, I might say, to have one's tongue curbed when others were quite unbridled. Hon. members will have learned from the press that Chief Judge Buchanan decided that protests against the membership of these persons from the Samson
1826	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry band of the Indian reserve were not properly made and that proceedings to have their names removed from the band list were therefore not valid. As soon as I heard of the judge's decision I made the following statement to the press:
I am delighted by Chief Judge Buchanan's decision because I have felt that these people, who have always been regarded as Indians, should continue to be regarded as Indians.
But I also felt it was my duty-
And I think it was the duty of every other member of this house.
-to carry out the law made by parliament and to give both sides in this dispute their day in court.
They have had it.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT
speechtext: It looks as though you have had it too.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
The statement continues:
I am only sorry the appeal was not made much sooner.
It will be evident to hon. members that if the appeal had been made to the courts as soon as the decision of the registrar was made, this case would have been settled several months ago without a great deal of unnecessary agitation and misrepresentation.
Ever since the act of 1951 was passed there has been, particularly in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, a persistent misrepresentation of the purposes of the provisions of the act which clarified the definition of an Indian and provided for the preparation of official band lists.
The Minister of Finance, when he was minister of citizenship and immigration, stated the purpose of these provisions to the special committee which was considering the bill, on April 12, 1951, in the following terms which I intend to read because I think it would be a good thing if the public knew what this bill really did:
We have provided in sections 6 to 15 of the bill-*
I am quoting Mr. Harris.
that there should be a new definition of "Indian" and that there should be a rather careful means of appeal from any decisions which have been made. We provide that band lists, which have been in the course of preparation since this recommendation-
That was the recommendation of a previous committee.
-and which are now practically complete, should be posted in the band council building or in the usual places where the band assembles, and that that list should be on display for a period of six months during which times appeals can be taken by any member of the band or band council to add names to the list or delete names from it.
The decision is made by the registrar who will be one of the officials from the department and within three months after that, an aggrieved person


or the band council may take appeal from his decision to a judge of the county or district court- presumably the one nearest to the band headquarters but not necessarily so, e.g., should there happen to be a vacancy in that appointment.
I am still quoting from Mr. Harris.
In this way, in the course of another year or something like that, we will have for the first time-
I emphasize those words, "for the first time".
-a more or less complete list of Indians. In so far as the lists are confirmed, they will not then-
And this is very important.
-be subject to change except for fraud, and of course there will be continuing additions and deletions by reasons of marriage, death and things of that sort.
In spite of that statement made at the time the bill was before parliament, it has been represented over and over again, particularly in one or two newspapers, that the purpose and effect of those amendments in 1951 has been to deprive a great number of people who were Indians of their Indian status, and that it is part of a systematic policy of expelling Indians from reservations. I believe hon. members would like to know what the facts really are.
Before the Samson case was settled, 359 other protests had already been settled and the number of persons confirmed in membership in Indian bands as a result of those protests was 1,732.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO INDIAN ACT

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF BAIT FROM NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that arises out of an incident last week when a Nova Scotia long liner was refused bait from one of the government bait depots in Newfoundland, and it
Inquiries of the Ministry illustrates the fact that though Newfoundland has now been in confederation almost eight years, custom dies hard. There are still Newfoundlanders who regard Canadians as foreigners and there are even some Nova Scotians who regard Newfoundlanders as foreigners.
Before confederation the government of Newfoundland operated a government bait depot service which supplied bait at less than cost to Newfoundland fishermen. Such bait of course was not sold to fishermen from other countries whether those countries were Canada, Portugal or any of the other nations that fish the Grand Banks. We in Canada have never had government bait depots. We have left the supplying of bait to private enterprise, to the fishing companies. We have encouraged the bait depot supply by offering a subsidy of $10,000 to any fishing company which would build with their cold storage plants a bait supply depot and supply bait to the fishermen at the going rates.
Under the terms of union, however, the government of Newfoundland insisted that we maintain the government bait depot service in Newfoundland without fundamental change and we have done that in Newfoundland. It costs us more than $300,000 a year. Because of the custom which had grown up of these bait depots serving only Newfoundland boats, and because Nova Scotians did not obtain bait there before confederation, it has been only in the last week or two that the problem has arisen.
I have issued instructions to all bait depots in Newfoundland to supply all Canadian fishing vessels with bait from these depots at the going price.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asked if I had been requested to investigate the reported importation into British Columbia of California potatoes which have been dyed red in order to create the impression that they are new potatoes.
In reply I may say that I am advised by the officials of my department that a small shipment of potatoes was received recently in Victoria, B.C., from the state of Nebraska, not California, which had been dyed red. The house resumed, from Friday, February 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 16, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company and certain wholly owned subsidiaries-Mr. Mcllraith-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
Clause 1 agreed to.
On clause 2-Railways and undertakings vest in Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether or not the sponsor is willing to drop the names of these two companies which were mentioned during the debate on second reading. If not, we feel that we should emphasize our desire in that respect by moving an amendment. As far as I am concerned, I placed my views before the house on second reading and I do not want to take up the time of the house at this moment. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I will move:
That section 2 be amended by deleting the words "the Kaslo and Slocan Railway Company" and the words "Nakusp and Slocan Railway Company".

Mr. Chairman, when this bill
was in committee previously, on February 22, the hon. member for Kootenay West and I explained why we were suggesting that these two particular subsidiaries be deleted from the bill. I have no intention of going over that submission in detail again today. However, for the benefit of those hon. members on both sides of the house who were not here on that occasion may I point out that these two subsidiaries-I refer to the Kaslo and Slocan Railway Company and the Nakusp arid Slocan Railway Company-are the owners of a short line of railway in the mountainous area of Kootenay West in respect of which the Canadian Pacific Railway was given permission about a month ago to abandon the line.
One of the conditions of that order was that the right of way must be conveyed to the provincial government before the abandonment could take effect, the reason behind that term of the order made by the board of transport commissioners being that they did not wish to have the residents of the district left without adequate transportation. It was felt that, although the railway line had to be abandoned,-with which conclusion I have some quarrel; I do not believe that order should have been made-the board of transport commissioners would take this step to see that at least there was a highway.
That was only a month ago. The C.P.R. has written to the provincial government about turning over the right of way. When

Private Bills
the bill was last under discussion the hon. member for Ottawa West told us that a reply had been received from the provincial government merely acknowledging the letter from the C.P.R. It will take a little time to work out this transfer of the right of way to the provincial government. Our only purpose in making the suggestion in this amendment today is that in that way public attention is focused on the need of the people in the district for a highway, and we are hoping that having attention so focused will result in much prompter action by both the railway and the provincial government to construct a proper highway over at least part of the right of way which is to be conveyed.
It is not as though the C.P.R. would suffer at all if they deleted these particular subsidiaries from the bill because they are working on a general program of taking over 36 or 37 subsidiaries; the hon. member for Ottawa West can correct that figure if I am wrong. Last year they put through a bill affecting 12 subsidiaries. This year I think there are 13 subsidiaries, or 12 again. The remainder will be dealt with at the session of 1958. Hence if these two were deleted from the present bill and then were included in the bill which will be before parliament next session, the final objective of the railway company would be attained; and by a delay of this kind we at least do something to help the people of the district get a highway to replace the railway. So far as these two lines are concerned this is really unfinished business, and we suggest that the two companies be not dissolved until that particular business has been completed.

As I said when this item was last before the committee, I cannot see that the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Kootenay West has any relevance to the bill before the committee. It is quite clear in the bill that all the obligations of the subsidiary companies are taken over by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Indeed, the order of the board of transport commissioners to which reference has been made is an order against the Canadian Pacific Railway. Since the point raised, and the whole argument, is quite irrelevant to the bill before the committee I am at a loss to understand the request to have the names of the two subsidiary companies deleted. Nothing has been said in argument relating the point raised by the hon. members to the bill before the committee.

Since that is the case, I regret that I can see no other course than to reject the amendment put forward.
On this question of delay, I think I ought to make it quite clear that there has been no delay on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and indeed, so far as we are aware, no delay on the part of the British Columbia government. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the condition is that as soon as the operation is abandoned the reconveyance is to be made. According to the order, the operation is abandoned as of February 1, 1957. The Canadian Pacific Railway started proceedings to convey the lands on February 6, 1957. If hon. members will look at their calendars they will see that a weekend intervened. They will see just how little delay there was. Since there is no delay and, so far as I know, no suggestion that there is any delay, I cannot see any point in even the irrelevant part of their argument. This being the case, I find myself in the unhappy position of having to respectfully differ from the two hon. members and reject their argument and ask that the amendment be voted down.

Before the question is put, there is one point of clarification I should like to get from the sponsor of the bill. Did I understand him to say that the lands have been transferred to the British Columbia government?

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fairey for the second reading of Bill No, 15, respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo).

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the explanatory note says:
The purpose of this bill is to subdivide each of the shares without nominal or par value into five shares without nominal or par value. The reason for the proposed subdivision is that the company wishes to achieve a wide distribution of its stock among investors in Canada. At January 8, 1957, the shares of the company had a market value of approximately $115 each. This relatively high market price discourages investment by small investors.
My colleagues who have spoken I think have established the point that the alleged reason for bringing this bill before parliament is not the real reason. It would appear to us that the sponsors of this proposition are really not concerned about the position of the small people in Canada.
When the bill was first before parliament in 1951 I find that the present sponsor, the Hon. Senator McKeen, had this to say in the Senate on February 20, 1951:
I may say that this is an all-Canadian route, and the pipe line will end in Canada.
The Bechtel organization which proposes to build this pipe line, and which is now asking for the charter, is one of the largest and best-equipped pipe line contracting firms in the world.
The company which will build this pipe line is set up in Canada, and will be financed in Canada. The parent body is the Bechtel organization, with headquarters in San Francisco.
This, hon. senators, is not a promotional effort; it is an actual project to be carried out by people who are in the oil pipe line business. All oil companies who wish to participate in the financing and the shipping of oil through this line may come in, and assurance has been given by many of the
Private Bills
major companies that they will use this line to transport their product to the Pacific coast.
There will be an issue of shares to those participating in the line and there will be debentures with warrants available to the general public in Canada.
Well, as my colleagues have pointed out, this line was completed and it has turned out to be a very profitable proposition. The Hon. Senator McKeen, in introducing this proposal this year, had this to say:
This is a very simple bill; its purpose is to subdivide each of the company's shares without nominal or par value. By subdividing these shares and issuing five for one a wide distribution will be ensured, and there will be greater participation by the general public. That is the only purpose of the bill.
I think it should be pointed out that although the legislation authorized the issuing of five million shares, only one and one-half million have been issued. I think this proves that the alleged reason is not the real reason. If this company is concerned about having more people participate all they have to do is to issue another three and one-half million shares. Of those shares which have been issued, again only 450,000, only one-third of those which have been issued have been made available to the general public in the country.
It seems clear that this alleged reason to get more people participating is merely a cloak, or a screen, which is put up to get this measure through parliament. I think we should have a look at what is happening to those who are interested in this. According to Moody's Industrials, Pacific Petroleums Limited has been listed as one of the large outfits which is interested in Trans Mountain Pipe Line, and Pacific Petroleums in turn were the sponsoring company of Westcoast Transmission. If you take a group of 1,000 people it would appear that that would represent about $2 million worth of production. It is as plain as A B C that if one person out of 1,000 takes for himself $1 million out of the production of Canada, as Mr. Tanner would appear to be doing if he were to sell now, then the other 999 persons have only another $1 million to distribute and that is the reason why our old age pensioners are limited to $480 per year while one citizen considers that he is entitled to have $1 million as his share of the production of Canada for one year.
We consider that all the people of Canada by their labours produce the gross national product. We have not suggested that the gross national product can be divided into 16 million equal shares because the wealth is constantly changing, but we do think the system which is apparently supported by the three other parties in this house who are supporting this legislation-a system that approves of grabbing as large a piece of the pie as you can regardless of the plight of old age and other pensioners and other groups on fixed incomes-is a position that does not deserve support.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the more we study this bill and its effects the more strongly we feel that it should not be passed by the House of Commons. There are those in the house who seem to think it is a good thing for a few individuals to make a lot of money but it is our view that when some people make money without working for it others work without getting paid for what they have produced. In our view the stock splitting arrangement proposed by the bill fits in with the current trend so far as oil and pipe line stocks are concerned and is designed to bring about a further increase in the wealth of the shareholders of this company. That increase in wealth must come from somewhere and we know that it will come out of the work, sweat and toil of our people.
We are opposed to devices of this kind which in effect impose a tax on the real wealth produced by our people for the benefit of a privileged few. It was brought out a few days ago in the question and answer period and also by a study that one can make of the appropriate legislation that gains of this kind are known as capital gains and therefore are not even subject to ordinary income tax. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because of our strong feeling of opposition to the bill I have risen for these few minutes to propose another amendment. Despite our opposition to the bill

we were willing to have its subject matter- but only its subject matter-considered by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Our proposal in that respect having been rejected by the house, we are left with no alternative but to oppose the bill outright. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden):
That Bill No. 15 be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Before you put the amendment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few more words on the bill. I feel that a great many people, including a great many members of the house, are content not to investigate the real results of the course of action proposed in this particular measure. We have been hearing a great deal in recent months of the dangers of inflation in our economy.
We have the government attacked by members on this side of the house for their alleged tight-money policy to control inflation. I do not intend to go into the merits or demerits of the government's policy in that regard. However, I would point out that it is not much good the government having a tight-money policy and it is not much good members of the official opposition denouncing that policy if at the same time they are prepared to condone actions which, if multiplied sufficiently, might well prove to be extremely serious inflationary factors.
We have a proposal at the present time which is, in short, a proposal to promote stock market gambling in the shares of a certain corporation. Let there be no other description of that proposal. I do not think anyone in this house seriously contends that this bill is intended to introduce new capital into this company. In fact, the necessity for introducing new capital into the company would now seem to be a highly debatable point considering the financial record of the company which has created the situation upon which these gentlemen wish to make their newer gains.
I think we can find the answer to this demand for melon cutting-for that is what it is-if we examine the latest statistical summary of the Bank of Canada. In this summary there is a table devoted to the index numbers of common stock prices covering the years 1955, 1956 and January of this year. It is notable that among the types of common stock that are listed here, there is one which is head and shoulders above all others when it comes to vast increase in the index number of the common stock prices,

and that is that of the oil companies. The oil companies' stocks in the last year have increased on the average, as indicated by this index column, in market price nearly 50 per cent across the board. We all know that these pipe line companies are in essence the creatures of the oil companies. They are usually closely connected with similar directorates and very often they are wholly-owned subsidiaries. However, that is where the money is obviously being made today.
It is notable that, in contrast with an almost 50 per cent increase in twelve months for oils, such an industry as the pulp and paper industry, which is usually considered to be one of our more profitable ones, has actually had a decline in the last year in the index number of stock prices. The same is true throughout almost the whole range.
Here I think we have the answer to this demand that these people be permitted to divide their stock by five. For what purpose do they want to do this? To take advantage of the anticipated increase again which will doubtless be revealed next year. When the Bank of Canada produces its statistical summary no doubt we shall see there that the same process which has been going on quite steadily for the over two years covered by this column will continue, and the fortunate gentlemen who have made five blades of grass grow where one grew before will be reaping a very heavy harvest of pay from the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It will be green stuff all right.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
It is green stuff, yes; and which they did not sow, as my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin suggests.
I want to deal again with the problem that I think every member of this house should take quite seriously, namely the dangers of encouraging and indeed permitting practices of this sort which are in essence invitations to stock market gambling. I think every hon. member should realize just what effect there may well be on our economy if this encouragement continues in these fields where these enormous gains are being made at the present time. There can be observed also from the report of the Bank of Canada the way in which those who deal in stocks borrow from the chartered banks for the purpose of their stock dealing; and every borrowing from the chartered banks is an inflationary factor in the economy.
We seem to consider it to be respectable to engage in and to encourage this type of gambling; yet, of course, we frown very severely on the old ladies who go and play
Private Bills
bingo every Saturday night. However, the old ladies who play bingo, if they are doing anything, are merely hurting themselves; but the gentlemen engaged in stock market gambling in the stratospheric area of the millions and billions of dollars are seriously endangering the livelihood of their fellow Canadians.
I want to stress again a point that I myself stressed earlier and that my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North stressed the other day, namely the illusion that so many people have that we may permit these gentlemen to make money, as the phrase is, without in any way affecting the economic position of their fellow Canadian citizens. I believe it is the use of that term "make money" that deludes people. There is only one agency in the country that makes money, namely our integrated central bank and the chartered banks. What the rest of us do, Mr. Speaker, is to attempt to collect money that is already in existence. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the use of the term "make money" suggests that in some way these people add something to the general well-being of the country when they, by manipulation, add a market value to their holdings of shares in these corporations whereas, of course, what they are doing is collecting claims on wealth that will buy just as much in the way of bacon and eggs as will the money that the wage earner gets in his pay cheque or the money that the salary earner gets in his salary; and the more they are permitted to accumulate, the less there will be for the rest of the economy.
Do not let us try to dodge away from that particular issue. They are given the right to accumulate claims on wealth and they can be held by only one person at a time. If A has these claims on wealth, B cannot have them. If A is an astute and acquisitive stock market operator and if B is a wage earner or an old age pensioner, then I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the only position for responsible representatives of the people to take is that the requirements of B-that is of the wage earner or the old age pensioner-[DOT] must be met before these ludicrous gains are permitted to people who engage in no useful occupation whatever. It is not the fact that they contribute anything whatever to the operation of these pipe lines; it is not the fact that they build the pipe line, manage the line or man the pipe line when it is in operation. They merely gamble on the claims on wealth that belong to the people of this country. For that reason I think that if this parliament is going to give encouragement to this type of gambling, with its serious dangers for the economy and its gross injustice to the vast majority of the people, then it will also be obliged to give consideration to the

Private Bills
possibility of clipping the wings of these gentlemen who make at present untaxable capital gains. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote against the adoption of this measure. I have not yet heard from those who have been supporting this bill a single argument that would persuade me that any honest and responsible representative of the people could do anything but vote against the bill. It is not going to promote more pipe lines. It is not going to result in an increase in wealth. It is merely going to result in a transfer of existing wealth into the hands of those who have done nothing to contribute to its production.

The bill seeks to remove the limitation which is placed on the amount of real estate that the army may hold. They have two separate divisions, one being -what is known as the governing council of the Salvation Army, Canada East, and the other the governing council of the Salvation Army, Canada West. The first council, that in eastern Canada, is in charge of the buildings from the Manitoba boundary east and has a limitation that was placed in 1916 of an annual value of real estate amounting to $350,000. That means, of course, that the annual rental or income value cannot be higher than $350,000. In the provinces west of the 82715-117

Manitoba-Ontario boundary the annual value of the real estate is set at $200,000.
Now, in the last three years the property held by the army has increased greatly in value. Furthermore, they have under way a development program which will amount to an expenditure of quite a large sum of money, I think $12 million. The result of this increase in the present value of the real estate and of the building program will be that the annual value of real estate will be very much higher than the figures which were set in 1916, and the army are asking that this limitation be removed entirely so that there will be no limit on the real estate they can hold.
They are also asking that the provision be made retroactive because apparently at the present time their real estate is over the figure allowed by their private statutes. May I point out that in recent years no other religious body has had a limitation of this kind placed in the charter.
I suggest it is entirely reasonable that the Salvation Army should be freed from that limitation.
Of course they have always done splendid work in Canada. I believe the work commenced in 1882. At the present time they have 35 hospitals and homes, three children's homes, 20 homes for aged men and women, 22 men's hostels and in addition they own places of worship and residences for their officers, training schools and other buildings. The properties are used to promote men's and women's social services, prison and court work, the relief of distress, fresh air camps and church work as an evangelical denomination. I understand they have social institutions such as industrial departments, general hospitals, maternity hospitals, girls' homes and eventide homes for aged men and women.
I personally came in contact with the Salvation Army in the first war and I believe that every Canadian veteran who returned from that war has nothing but good words to say concerning the work of the Salvation Army. I know they have carried on in that same wonderful way in British Columbia and I presume in other parts of Canada as well. speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 207, respecting Canadian Co-operative Credit Society Limited.
Explain.

This bill is of a technical character designed to permit the Co-operative Credit Society of Manitoba Limited to become a member of the Canadian Cooperative Credit Society Limited as was intended by parliament when the Canadian society's act of incorporation was passed in 1953.
Under the Co-operative Credit Associations Act membership is limited to provincial credit societies which are declared to be eligible by an act of parliament and which also meet the statutory requirements for certification by the treasury board. The Manitoba society was declared eligible to become a member by the act incorporating the Canadian society in 1953, but was not able to meet all the technical requirements for certification within the three-year time limit imposed by the Co-operative Credit Associations Act.
The Manitoba society is now in a position to comply with these requirements and desires to become a full participant in the Canadian society, and the purpose of this bill is to make it again eligible to become a member of the Canadian society. Because the bill involves no principle and is of such a technical character, it is eminently suitable for discussion in committee when representatives of both credit societies and the superintendent of insurance will be available to answer questions.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I have asked the hon. member for Vancouver South, because of his practical common sense, to support this resolution. I have raised this question in the house twice a year for the last three years, in the debate on the speech from the throne and during the discussion of the budget.
We place it before the consideration of hon. members now for two reasons; first because of the need; and second, because I believe when the government sees the need, when that need touches human lives, and when it is all-Canadian, the government rises to the occasion and the need is satisfied.
I can prove this contention from the record of the government over the last 20 years or more, but I will just use one example. I had a resolution up for three years dealing with the handicapped. When the government saw the need, after the last election, they passed a bill dealing with the handicapped.
This resolution is very simple. It deals with men and women who gave long service in the armed forces, in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and in the civil service at a time when wages were low. Conditions of service then were not what they are today. There was no 40-hour week; people had to work ten hours a day. One section of the civil service, the postmen, were on duty six days a week, and when snow was on the streets and the streets were not cleared they often worked more than ten hours a day, though they never received any overtime pay.
When I think of the need, I think of people I know. I get my information not from the press or from members of parliament but from my own experience and as a result of my own investigations at first hand. I have known men who have cut out certain luxuries because they could no longer afford them. One man had to give up smoking his pipe. When I was a boy they used to say that the two great comforts of a man were his pipe and his wife. So in cutting out his pipe he had cut out one of his main comforts. It occurs to me that if some members of this house had to give up smoking their pipes they would be kicking like an irritated mule. When a man has to give up a luxury like that, it hurts him. But a man who can do something like this to enable his wife or companion to have the necessities of life must be big enough, and is surely deserving of our help.
The United Kingdom have dealt with this matter, and we plan our legislation along largely the same lines as the United Kingdom does. In 1920 they increased their pensions,

in 1924 they increased their pensions, in 1944 they increased their pensions, in 1947 they increased their pensions and on April i, 1956, they increased their pensions. They did so because men and women in different classes of employment had different types of salaries, and the British government felt that it was necessary to deal with them as the years went along.
The United States have a different type of government but they too have increased their pensions and, like the United Kingdom, they have made an attempt to examine the whole situation and ascertain on the basis of justice what would be a just, decent and reasonable minimum standard for those civil servants who retired on low pensions.
I am told that the average pension is $60 a month. There are some retired civil servants who had big salaries and they would get larger pensions, but those under $60 a month are greater in numbers than those above. The average pension for widows is $20 a month. When we think of the need of these men and women surely we shall rise to the occasion. I should like to read a portion of a letter from Mr. S. Carberry of the association of superannuated civil servants of Manitoba. This is what he says:
The purchasing power today is worth less than half that amount.
He means less than half what it was when these people retired.
When the government of 1924 brought into force the Superannuation Act, it stated the main reason for doing so was that it wished their retired civil servants not to be dependent on charity. It seems unfair that superannuated civil servants who have laboured through the years and helped to establish a pension or superannuation allowance find that it is not sufficient to maintain themselves now.
I know it is not sufficient. When a small boy I was told by a great Scotsman that the light that shines farthest shines brightest at home. The retired civil servants belong to the big family of the government of Canada. We can see this dark spot which is helping to blur the light of this great Canada of ours, and as long as we allow this situation to exist we know it is going to hurt all Canada.
To sum up briefly, many of these retired civil servants had a salary of $120 a month. Today workers in the same positions would get $300 a month or close to it, and with far better conditions of work. Many of these retired civil servants are getting $60 a month or less, and their pensions should be doubled. We put this situation before the government and in considering the question today I am sure the government will not put the matter off until after the election but will grant relief to these people, some of whom are not

getting three meals a day. We see the need and so does all of Canada. I thank the government in anticipation of their granting this request.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the official opposition are very glad to support the motion, which is in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants who were retired when salaries were low, so as to bring such pensions more in line with those of the present.
In moving his motion the hon. member for Fort William has said that the government always meets the need. Of course he has great faith in the government; I think far more than most of the members on the government side of the house.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext: I have reason to.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
This is one case in which the government has been a long, long, long time meeting the need. I remember the demands for action of this type that were made in the house as far back as 1949. In that year both the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself urged just such action as is envisaged in this notice of motion. These demands have been made every year since, but the government has never seen fit to move one inch.
This year the Minister of Finance has again made a statement which certainly does not give much hope. On January 14 he was asked a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about the plight of the superannuated civil servants and, as found at page 166 of Hansard, this was his answer:
We have considered the question of superannuated civil servants and their pensions at some considerable length, Mr. Speaker, and have had discussions with various groups of persons who would be interested in it, including a deputation from the superannuated civil servants themselves. I do not want anyone to conclude from this that any action is imminent because these things are only announced in due course, if they are announced at all.
That was not a very hopeful statement and, Mr. Speaker, I believe the attitude of the government on this question has been not only indifferent but also absolutely and utterly
Pensions
callous. This need should have been met a long time ago. In my opinion Canadians today have the finest civil service in the world. I do not think our service has to take second place to that of any other country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
It has been built up in large degree by these men and women who have retired on very small superannuation. Practically all these retired civil servants spent their lives working for this country. They had no relationship with private firms. This is a situation directly involving the government and its own ex-employees. These Canadians can look in no other direction than to the government for a solution of this problem, which is not a problem of their own making.
They made their contributions to the superannuation fund from their salaries in the belief that when they retired their superannuation would be sufficient to enable them to carry on in the way to which they had been accustomed. No one can contradict that statement. The deductions taken from their salaries down through the years were such that these civil servants were entitled to believe that when they retired their superannuation would be of a value equivalent to the value of money at the time they made their payments.
I am sure the Minister of Finance will not contradict the assertion that civil service salaries were extremely low until recently. I have here an example of a collector of customs, who retired in 1937. At that time he was getting a salary of $2,600 a year. The man occupying his position today is getting $5,000 a year. Yet the man who retired in 1937 of course draws superannuation based only on the salary he was getting at that time. The cost of living has increased. It is increasing now every month. These worthy Canadians are caught in the squeeze.
I have here from the wife of one of the civil servants a letter which sets out the situation clearly. She says:
During the war years no increases were granted, income tax, etc. jumped and people like my husband, forced to retire due to ill-health (wartime overwork) were and are very hard hit. The money paid in during working years was worth its value, 100 cents to the dollar; present value less than one-third. We are only one of many in this situation, and a large percentage very much worse off than we are.
The other day we were given the figures as to the pensions paid by the government. These figures are to be found at page 1272 of Hansard and were given in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). He asked these questions:
How many are receiving monthly pensions of (a) $1,000 or more;-

Pensions
The answer to that question was "nil".
-	(b) between $500 and $999-
And the answer was "28".
-	(e) between $100 and $499-
And the answer was "7,067".
-	(d) between $40 and $99-
And the answer was "8,618".
-	(e) less than $40?
And the answer was "5,644". Then the third part of the question was:
3. What is the average pension paid in each of these groups?
When you look at the average in these groups the picture is even worse, because in paragraph (c) of the answer we find that in the group who were getting between $100 and $499 the monthly average is nothing like $499; it is $165.59. In the group getting between $40 and $99 the average again is nothing like $99; it is $67.61; and in the group getting less than $40-that is 5,644-the average is only $21.03.
Mr. Speaker, those pensions must be brought more in line with those of the present day. Other governments and many corporations have recognized that need. The hon. member for Fort William referred to the United Kingdom. I think his figures went away back before the second war. In any event some of them did. But I believe the United Kingdom has raised these pensions to superannuated civil servants several times within the last few years. The Americans have done the same thing. Some of the provinces of Canada have also raised these pensions to their superannuated civil servants. The Canadian Pacific Railway is one corporation which has done the same thing. The government will therefore not be setting any precedent if it moves to make some provision for the superannuated federal civil servants. They will be a long way down the line in the list of those who will have received the treatment to which they are so justly entitled.
Their requests have been supported by the civil service associations representing the men and women still in the civil service. It is not a question of the civil servants of today objecting to the superannuated civil servants receiving some additional benefits. These present-day civil servants for years have been demanding that the superannuated civil servants be treated fairly. For example, I have here a clipping under date of March, 1954, three years ago, which sets out that for two years prior to that time the civil service organizations had been requesting action of this type.
I have referred to the stand taken in the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, by myself and by many others.

Last year the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew, made a very strong speech urging action such as that which is urged in this notice of motion before the house today. The present Leader of the Opposition dealt with the matter in the only way in which he could do so, namely by a question, on January 18, to be found at page 387 of Hansard. On that occasion, questioning the Prime Minister, he said:
Can the Prime Minister assure the house that any increase in that regard to meet the continuing depreciated value of the dollar will be extended to the superannuation payments to retired civil servants, members of the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?
The Prime Minister replied and then the Leader of the Opposition asked a further question:
I then asked the Prime Minister whether the interpretation placed on the optimistic words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare yesterday is well founded because, after all, the minister chose to indicate that something was going to be done; and he having indicated that, certainly X think I have the right to ask whether similar treatment is going to be extended to those whom I have mentioned that find themselves in a serious plight.
We are in deadly earnest about this question on the opposition side of the house.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext: So are we.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
The actions of the government do not show it, even though the hon. member for Fort William may be very earnest about it and I am not doubting that he is.
The suggestions as to the manner in which this could be done will be varied. I had one suggestion put up by the superannuated federal civil servants of British Columbia in a letter dated January 11, 1957, which is subsequent to the opening of the house. In that letter they made this suggestion:
The only alternative therefore that suggests itself is to grant a measure of relief in the form of a flat rate bonus, thus giving the larger percentage benefits to those in the lower brackets whose need is the greater.
That may or may not be a sound suggestion, but it is put forward by that particular organization of superannuated federal civil servants which, of course, is made up of those drawing superannuation in varying amounts.
One might go on arguing at great length in support of this motion, but I do not believe it needs argument of that type, Mr. Speaker, because it is so obvious the government must stop dragging its feet on this question and take steps to meet this need. As I pointed out before, these civil servants who served Canada in the past had a very clear understanding. That understanding was the basis of the superannuation act itself when it was first introduced, that they would

receive a stated percentage of their pay when they retired, which would be sufficient for them to maintain approximately the same standard of living they had reached when they retired. What is needed today is that we bring about a closer relationship between current salary rates and these superannuation benefits.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance will be able to give us some statement in the course of this debate which will be a great deal more promising than the statement he made on January 14.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the introduction of this resolution. We are glad, too, that the Minister of Finance is in the house for this debate. We hope he will take part in it. I may say we hope for even more than that; we hope that in the course of whatever contribution he makes to this debate he will give us the assurance that something is going to be done about this question at this session.
Other hon. members have referred to the great number of questions that have been asked on this matter across the years. Indeed, if one were to put them all on the record there would not be much time left to make a new speech on this question. I have been encouraged, however, by the fact that the Minister of Finance has not answered the questions that have been asked at this session on this matter. In previous sessions this minister and his predecessors have referred us back to previous answers. This process simply turned one back to refusal after refusal to meet requests for an increase in the pensions of civil servants already retired.
This year, however, I could not help but notice that the Minister of Finance put me off on one pretext or another. I do not quarrel with his having done that. I take hope from the fact that he did not say no again this year, as he has done on previous occasions. It may be that before the session is over the answer will be yes. That is my hope.
I even take hope from the fact that a government member, the hon. member for Fort William, has placed this resolution on the order paper. Not only has he placed it on the order paper but he has moved it, and it is now before the house for consideration.
I trust that the rumours that are around that there are going to be increases in social security benefits of one kind and another are correct, and that when these increases come through they will include increases in
Pensions
the pensions of retired civil servants, particularly those whose plight we have been laying before the government for these many years.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra who has joined in these requests across the years, suggested that he and I, at any rate, have been asking for action on this matter as far back as 1949. In looking the matter over a few days ago I found that it goes back still farther. It goes back at least to 1947. I have in my hand a copy of Hansard for February 17, 1947, which is a little over 10 years ago. I find on page 469 of Hansard for that day these questions;

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
1.	Has consideration been given by the government to increasing the pensions of superannuated federal civil servants by the addition of a cost of living bonus or other supplement?
The answer was given by Mr. Mayhew, then the parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance, and the answer was "Yes".
My second question was in these words:
2.	If so, what is the result of such consideration? Is the matter receiving attention at the present time?
This is the answer the then parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance gave on behalf of the government on February 17, 1947:
This question is still receiving consideration and the government's policy will be announced in due course.
Ten years have gone by and many of the people on behalf of whom we pleaded in 1947, and in the succeeding years, have since passed away. Those who have managed to live during the years on the miserably small pensions that some of them are receiving have accomplished a miracle. I hope that at long last the announcement that was to be made in due course, as indicated back in 1947, will soon be forthcoming.
The hon. member for Fort William gave a few figures. He made reference, in fact, to what he called an average pension for retired civil servants. I do not believe anyone in this house needs to be warned against the use of averages. I think it is more significant to place on the record once again some figures as to the number of retired civil servants who have to get by on pensions which, by today's standards, are ridiculously small. There is still on this year's order paper a question of mine which would bring this information up to date, and no doubt this question will be answered soon. In the meantime, the latest information in this field can be found on page 785 of Hansard for February 1, 1956. On this page hon. members will find a lengthy table giving the number of retired civil

Pensions
servants and the number of widows drawing pensions in the various categories.
It is not my purpose to put all these figures on the record again, but I would draw attention to the fact that 2,710 retired civil servants are drawing pensions of less than $50 per month. This includes 355 retired civil servants who are drawing pensions of less than $20 per month. It is cold comfort to the people down in those brackets to be told that the average pension is $60 a month, as if even that were adequate. The same table shows that there are 4,196 widows of civil servants who are drawing pensions of less than $50 a month. This figure includes 1,077 widows who are drawing pensions of less than $20 per month. The total number of retired civil servants drawing pensions, according to the information given a year ago, was 13,022. The total number of widows of civil servants drawing pension at that time was 6,459.
These tables, and others, will support the contention which is sometimes made by the government that those who have retired in recent years, particularly if they were employed for a normal length of time and hence were able to take advantage of the amendments made recently to the Public Service Superannuation Act, are doing fairly well.
One does not deny that. I for one am prepared to give credit to the government for the improvements that have been made in recent years in the Public Service Superannuation Act; but our complaint, Mr. Speaker, is that during the time improvements were being made in the act for the benefit of those who were still working, nothing has been done by this government to improve the position of those who had retired previous to the occasion of such amendments. That includes quite a few people whose retirement dates back over a number of years, or whose pensions are based on salaries that were earned a number of years ago when those salaries were low. As former employees of the government they are just as deserving, they are just as human and just as needy as any other group of federal civil servants, and for the life of me I cannot understand the approach of the government that refuses to do anything for this particular group of its former employees.
A headline in tonight's paper reads, "Up Pay of 6,000 Ottawa Civil Servants". On the same front page is another headline reading, "Living Cost Rises Again". One is in 72 point type and the other is in 36 point type. Of course the one in the smaller type will catch up with everybody. My point is that the government does face up to some of the problems of the people who work for it. It

does face up sooner or later to problems as to the wage and salary rates of its employees, and it does do something through the years with regard to the Public Service Superannuation Act, looking to the future; but in all these changes that have been made this other group has been left out in the cold. Nothing has been done for them, although through the years that some of us have been pleading their case in this house many of them have died off.
I certainly hope this 10 year effort on our part is at last going to bear some fruit. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Fort William have pointed out that there are many people who support the contention that something should be done for these people. They have their own organizations in a number of centres across Canada. There is one in Quebec city; there are some of them in Montreal; there are some of them here in Ottawa and in Toronto who are organized, and there is a very active organization in Winnipeg. There are active organizations of retired civil servants in Vancouver and Victoria, and perhaps in other parts of British Columbia as well.
These people are not only presenting their own case; they have the support of other bodies. I note in particular that in the brief presented to the government of Canada on January 23 of this year by the Canadian Labour Congress a request was made on behalf of retired civil servants. It is to be found on page 31, where President Jodoin and the other members of that delegation made this request:
Adjustments should be made in the pensions of retired civil servants to replace their purchasing power.
The point should be noted that a body such as the Canadian Labour Congress, like others, is concerned not only for those who are still working, not only for the pension plans which are still being built up, but are concerned about the plight of those who are already retired, who are forgotten by their former employers, but who are just as deserving Canadians as any other group in our society.
I should like to point out once again that other jurisdictions have done something about this matter. Mr. Abbott, prior to the present Minister of Finance, and Mr. Ilsley before him, one by one have stood up time and again and argued that this was a contractual arrangement, this was something that the government could do nothing about. The contention has been that these people get what they are entitled to by virtue of the amount of time they worked and the amount of money they paid in.

I remind the government again that other jurisdictions have dealt with this matter. The hon. member for Fort William must have read one of my former speeches, in view of the dates he was quoting today. In the case of the United Kingdom, for many years it has been the practice of the government of that country, under all the parties that have- been in power, to provide pension increases not only for those still in the service but for those already retired, the value of whose pensions had decreased because of the rising cost of living, or decreased in relation to the rising standard of living.
The United States federal government has taken action along this line; likewise many of the state governments have taken action to raise the pensions of retired civil servants. At least two provinces in this country, Newfoundland and Saskatchewan, have taken action to increase generally the pensions of their retired civil servants. In addition the province of Ontario has taken action with respect to its retired teachers. Teachers' pensions in the province of Ontario are not too bad, but even that province recognizes that in the case of those who retired prior to a few years ago conditions have changed, the cost of living has gone up, and their pensions would not meet today's conditions and today's standard of living, and so in their case improvements have been made.
A number of private companies have taken action along this line. Some of them are not too magnanimous in what they have done, but at least some changes have been made.
I confess that in one or two cases of which I am aware advantage is taken by such companies of the Old Age Security Act. In other words, those increases apply only up until age 70; but there are other instances where a genuine and permanent improvement in the pensions of retired civil servants has been made. Therefore it is not a new idea, Mr. Speaker; it is not a radical departure to request that something like this be done. It is just one of the facts of life that other governments and other employers have faced, but which this government seems to feel it does not need to worry about.
I am reminded, of course, of the fact that the same questions and answers to which I referred, as found on page 785 of Hansard for February 1, 1956, include information as to the distribution of our retired civil servants and their widows across Canada. I find that they are scattered in all the various provinces. There are only 79 retired civil servants in Newfoundland; there are 616 in Manitoba, and 2,159 in British Columbia. I am not going to give all the figures. I do this just to indicate that these people do
Pensions
not constitute a large block in any one area or, shall I say, in any one constituency where they could wield any great political influence. I must confess that there are times when some of us have felt that maybe that was the reason we could not get action out of this government, the fact that they were too small and too scattered a group. Mr. Speaker, I plead that any such consideration-

speechtext: Is that the hon. gentleman's standard?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
No, it is not my standard, and precisely because they are so small a group they do not affect anybody's vote in any constituency represented in this house either for or against a particular member. There are very few in any single member's constituency. But I am suggesting that it strikes some of us that this may be one of the reasons they have not received better consideration at the hands of the government.
I say again I hope that the straws in the wind do tell us which way the wind is blowing and that this year, when things are being done just before a certain event that is not far off, one of the things that will be done will be the provision of a long needed and long deserved increase in the pensions of our retired civil servants.
One of the arguments that has been used repeatedly, of course, is that our civil servants draw their pensions by virtue of a contract, and that so long as the government lives up to that contract it is doing all it needs to do.
Like the Minister of Finance in a speech he was making the other day I am reluctant to quote myself-one is reluctant to go back and read a speech that one made on a former occasion-but maybe I will get caught in the same trap he got caught in and find myself doing it before I am through.
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to do that, but I would like to remind the Minister of Finance of a quotation I read to him in a former debate from the Hansard of the United Kingdom. This was on February 21, 1956, in this house as reported at pages 1418 and 1419, when I drew his attention to a debate that had taken place on this matter in the parliament at Westminster on March 3, 1944. The particular quotation which I drew to the attention of the Minister of Finance then I think is one that bears repeating to him now. The quotation is from Mr. Pethick-Lawrence, a Labour member of the British house in 1944, who was supporting the coalition government of that day which on that occasion was bringing in an

Pensions
increase in the pensions of retired civil servants. Mr. Pethick-Lawrence had this to say:
I would like now to say a word on the broad facts. I am in agreement with the Chancellor of the Exchequer that legalistically interpreted the public pensioner has no precise right to any increase in his pension. The strict law of his contract has been kept,-
I break in, Mr. Speaker, to remind you how often that has been said to us in this house. Mr. Pethick-Lawrence said, if I may continue:
-but the fact is that underlying all contracts for payment at some future date there is an assumption, unwritten and unspecified, but nevertheless implied. That is the stability of the purchasing power of money. Unless this is substantially maintained all time-contracts are meaningless.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext: Do you agree with that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Yes. Precisely because the government does not maintain the purchasing power of money it cannot insist that these time contracts such as we are talking about now have to remain unchanged through the years. Further on in the same speech Mr. Pethick-Lawrence said this:
There is this further point when we are dealing with employees of the state. A private employer may argue that he had nothing to do with fixing the value of money, that it is an act of God so far as he is concerned, God being the state or possibly the Chancellor of the Exchequer.
When the state makes a contract, however, it itself has the power of altering the value of money, and, therefore, the state cannot quite get away with that excuse. Therefore, I have come to the conclusion and I think it is the same conclusion to which the Chancellor has come, although he may not have put it quite so bluntly, that in equity the state must review its contracts to meet the situation.
That is what the hon. member for Fort William is asking for in his resolution. That is what some of us on this side of the house have been asking for ten long years.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext: Twelve.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver East says 12; I do not doubt we have been asking for this action for even longer, but it just so happens that I have the record before me going back for 10 years.
Mr. Speaker, that is what we are asking for now, that the state as represented by the government across the way review its contracts with these old and deserving employees to meet the situation which they now face. They cannot and should not be asked to live on pensions of the size some of them are receiving. I make that plea not only in the light of the higher cost of living which as I say, according to this evening's Ottawa Journal, is still going up; I make it because we feel that as time goes by and 
as society improves its standard of living generally, our older people have a right to share in that improvement even though they may riot be working at that particular time.
A pension is not just the right to retire and be kept alive in a state of mere existence. A pension should be-and several writers on the subject whose works I have scattered on the desk before me have made this clear- a person's claim on a share of the standard of living in the society he has helped to build. This applies to all our older people. It applies to all our older citizens and old age pensioners generally with equal force, but in this particular instance we are thinking of the government as an employer.
The government does have these two functions. It is the maker of legislation affecting the people generally, and it is the authority that can impose taxes for redistributing wealth amongst our people generally. But it is also an employer, and as such it has a responsibility to its former employees which we feel has not been fully met.
I have no hesitation in saying to the Minister of Finance that the government of which he is a member deserves credit for the improvements it has made in the Public Service Superannuation Act. It is a much better piece of legislation today than it was 10 years ago, but it is better only for those who are still working and who can take advantage of the improvements that have been made in that act. In the meantime nothing has been done to improve the situation of any persons who were retired prior to the amendments that improved the Public Service Superannuation Act.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I remind the minister that on one former occasion-I believe it was last year; yes, on July 17, 1956-I pointed out to him that some people have been giving study to this matter and have made concrete suggestions as to changes that might be made in the act to take care of this problem in the years that lie ahead.
The minister would probably say to me that if we improve the position of these people I have referred to in the statistics, what about 10 years from now? That is a good question. Ten years from now those who are presently benefiting from a pretty good Public Service Superannuation Act may find that the situation has deteriorated and that they will not be doing as well then as they now believe will be the case.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I will finish in about five minutes when we return at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
