speechtext:
In 1935 I had the great honour of helping to elect to the house the hon. member for Fort William and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe).
Before I get into the subject matter of the resolution I think I should spend a few minutes on the question of private members' resolutions, especially private members' resolutions originating from the government side. In the years I have been here I know that many times I have been on the horns of a dilemma. At times there have been resolutions or even bills originating from the opposition side and I have found myself in the uncomfortable position of either having to vote for them, seemingly against the government, or of being forced to take a passive attitude which was rather contrary to my general long-range inclinations.
I want to point out what I think is one of the mistakes we make in the house. I believe that private members' resolutions, regardless of where they originate, should be considered entirely on their merits. They should be considered entirely on the basis of the terms in which they are framed. Since I have been thinking about the matter I have been looking into the past history of occurrences in the house over the years. I think anyone who looks into the great political career of the present senator from Quebec, Chubby Power, over the years when he was a private member almost always sitting on the side of the government, can find plenty of evidence of a robust independence, and even of the initiation or suggestion of things which were not yet government policy.
If we go back farther into history we can find the most famous case of all involving a member on the Conservative benches in the days when there was a Conservative government headed by Sir Robert Borden. At that time the then Conservative member for Kingston City introduced his famous resolution calling for the abolition of titles. The more I think of that the more I think what a tremendous feat of moral courage it must have been for a Conservative private member sitting on the government side of the house to move a resolution calling for the abolition of titles when his own leader, the then prime minister of Canada, bore a famous title honoured over the whole world and when the leader of the Liberal opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was equally distinguished in that regard.
Pensions
So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest that in my opinion it would be of advantage to the work of the house if we did not go beyond the terms of the resolutions themselves, and if there was a disposition on the part of the opposition as well as the government to treat these private members' resolutions entirely on their merits and not try to read into them things which are not there.
Mr. Speaker, to me this seems to be perhaps not one of the great world-shaking issues with which we are called upon to deal every now and then, or perhaps one not even in the major league with regard to social welfare. We know that even this week we are going to be called upon to deal with one of the great forward steps in the setting up of a better social security system in Canada when we get around to dealing with the latest great achievement of this government, sparked by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), when he brings in his national hospital insurance scheme. Some of us have even greater hopes in connection with another matter which I will not mention right at the moment for fear of being called out of order. However, I am still hoping that we shall reach it on my resolution if we get around to having another day's discussion on private members' motions. As I say, Mr. Speaker, this is perhaps not one of the great major issues. However, I think it is an important issue.
I believe the government should give every possible consideration to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Fort William, above all for two reasons. I believe the government-and for that matter this whole house-* has a double responsibility to see that the lower-paid retired civil servants have their pensions brought up to something like equality with the pensions of those who have retired at a later date. I remember, Mr. Speaker, when I had the sad duty last year of having to carry on some of the unfinished business of the late hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the late Dr. Jack MacDougall, and when on his behalf I had the great privilege of raising a matter which he had promised to raise, namely the pensions of retired C.P.R. men who were getting less than a living pension.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, how members on all sides of this house lent the full weight of their moral support to the suggestion that the C.P.R. was at least morally bound to give a living pension to the men who had borne the heat and burden of their operations in the earlier years before the value of money had begun to go down. I know that in my capacity as a private member of parliament

Pensions
or, for that matter, even before I was a member of parliament, I more than once had to write to the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, asking for this same general reform with regard to C.N.R. pensioners who were drawing less than a living pension, in some cases because of war services which took them out of service in the years they would have made their contribution to build it up to enable them to get a living pension when they retired.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is a good principle that you should never suggest to anybody else that he should do a thing if you yourself are not willing to do that same thing. It seems to me that we who are members of parliament have at least a moral obligation to see that the employees of this great Dominion of Canada have all the rights of employment that a good private employer would give to those same employees. I therefore think we, as members of parliament or as members of the government, have a moral obligation which is above and beyond the strict letter of the law with regard to pensions.
But, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we also have a larger responsibility, those of us who sit in this house. While it is not through any fault of the government, and not through any fault of this parliament or of any one party in this parliament, the fact remains that since the beginning of the second world war the purchasing value of money has steadily gone down year by year. I think anyone can make out a convincing argument to prove that when these people were making their contributions to the pension fund they were paying in dollars worth so much in eggs, so much in bacon, or so much in oatmeal porridge if you will. I think we have at least a moral obligation to see that they get out of their pension repayments something equivalent in value to what they paid in.
In the years that I have been a backbencher of this House of Commons I have sometimes sat here in amazement at the fact that, as far as I can find out, everybody in this house is in favour of higher prices. Many a day I have sat here and looked around this house and asked myself this question: Where are the people in this House of Commons who favour lower prices on everything? All the talk I hear year after year, month after month and even week after week is about higher prices. In fact I heard it only three quarters of an hour ago in a television broadcast, which I saw in the next room, about the necessity for higher supports right across the board to keep prices up.

My point is this. I am certainly not criticizing the government for the fact that we had a second world war, or that we had a cold war which followed the second world war and forced this country into a vast rearmament program which had the indirect effect of lowering the purchasing value of our money. But I am suggesting this. As this parliament as a whole is responsible for the fact that the purchasing power of the money has been allowed to fall-for very good reasons; for reasons which we could not avoid- we therefore have a double obligation. Over and above our short-range obligation to the men and women who have served this country well we have a larger national obligation to those same civil servants because of economic upsets and economic deficiencies over which they have no control.
As I know that there are many others who wish to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker,
I do not intend to prolong my argument, except to say that it is a great honour for me to give the fullest possible moral support to the fine resolution moved by my venerable friend the hon. member for Fort William.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants who were retired when salaries were low, so as to bring such pensions more in line with those of the present.
It seems to me amazing, Mr. Speaker, that it should be necessary to call the government's attention to such a worthwhile resolution. Surely the government has been giving consideration to this matter. Members on this side of the house for years have spoken about the necessity of providing some additional pension to those civil servants who were retired years ago. There have been letters written by the superannuated federal civil servants' association; therefore it comes as a shock to me to think that a member on the front benches on the government side, who must be in close touch with what the government is thinking, who must attend the caucuses of the Liberal party and must have heard the proposals which were made by the various cabinet ministers, should find it necessary to introduce this resolution. I would have hoped that this matter had received consideration, and that before the end of this session some definite pronouncement would be made which would have ensured a substantial increase in the pensions of those who have retired, in some cases many years ago when their pensions were very small and the cost of living was very low.
I have a letter from the superannuated federal civil servants of Vancouver which was

written at the beginning of this year, and which respectfully requests that the superannuation act be amended so as to provide a closer relationship between current salary rates and superannuation benefits presently being paid to those retired. Then the letter goes on:
It is obviously unfair to place retired civil servants and widows of civil servants who are more or less unemployable into a position of semidestitution through the reduction of the purchasing power of the dollar-
Then this is put in block letters.
-a condition never contemplated by government or anyone else when provisions of the superannuation act were drawn up.
I do not think I need to emphasize the point that the cost of living has gone up. We know that if you take 1939 as the basic year equalling 100, by 1949 the cost of living index had gone up to 186. Then there was a revision in the cost of living index, and it was based on 1949 equalling 100. Still this index has been going up, and I noticed that according to tonight's paper there has been a further increase. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of this day's date:
Living costs rose again in January, pushing the consumer price index to a record 120.5, an increase of one fifth of a point from 120.3 in December.
The article goes on to set out the main causes for such an increase. Over the week end it was being pointed out by Ottawa newspapers that a survey had been made to ascertain the actual conditions under which superannuated civil servants in this city were living. Earlier in the year the Victoria Daily Colonist carried out a survey in my own city in order to examine how some of the old civil servants were able to exist on the very small pensions they were receiving. So it may be really brought home to us in this house, let me quote from the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, March 2:
A growing minority of Ottawa residents contrive to live on an income far below the level necessary for "marginal" comfort. Age, for them, has brought the indignity of daily bread in small, measured doses.
A Journal survey has shown without doubt that extreme hardship is the daily lot of many pensioners and superannuated civil servants in the lower income brackets. Forced by circumstance to retire from the active earning force, these "senior citizens" are losing ground month by month in a tragic struggle to make ends meet. They are in fact underprivileged citizens caught hopelessly in the spiral of rising living costs.
We are all conscious of rising living costs and the inflation which faces us at the present time. We know that some attempts have been made by the government to check this inflation. After having given it the original impetus by the tremendous spending of the various government departments, they are frantically trying to adjust the brakes in
Pensions
order to stop the runaway car to which they gave the original push. However, inflation is here, and something has got to be done for these senior retired civil servants.
If the government is not able to check inflation, then it seems to me only fair and just that the government must find some other means of helping those who are really the underprivileged class of the nation. I could read a number of letters I have received from Vancouver island during this session pointing out the plight of these people, but I shall not take up the time of the house by doing so. I merely repeat that these elderly men and women who have served this country in numerous capacities in the past are now in desperate straits. It is only by increasing their pension at the present time that some measure of relief can be brought to them, until such time as a government is able to check this inflationary trend.
I say "some measure", because other governments have been able to devise some means by which assistance could be given to retired public servants. As has already been pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, steps were taken in the United Kingdom to increase the pensions not only of civil servants but of ex-servicemen, the personnel of the regular navy, army and air force. The United Kingdom has found means by which their pensions could be increased. Substantial increases have been granted to retired pensioners in the United States. I believe that even in our own country there are schemes in certain provinces whereby provincial civil servants who had gone on superannuation some years ago were to receive a cost of living bonus which amounted to so much per month for every year of service before a certain date.
If it is possible for other countries which are not nearly as wealthy as our country, and for several provinces, to look after their superannuated civil servants, surely it should be within the realm of possibility for this government, with its enormous surplus, to find some means before this session is over of relieving the dire hardship in which many of these elderly citizens are living.
I noticed that when the hon. member for Fort William introduced this resolution he did not confine himself to its actual wording as it appears on the order paper, but he extends the provisions he was suggesting to include ex-members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and ex-members of the regular forces of this country who had been making their contributions in the past. I will say only this, that of all the pension schemes which have been in existence, that which paid pensions to the Royal Canadian

Pensions
Mounted Police, or the Royal North-West Mounted Police, as they were before, was the most unsatisfactory of all.
There are many ex-members of that great force who are today living in very straitened circumstances because when they were carrying out their duties of maintaining order throughout western Canada they were on very small pay and allowances, and the pensions were based on those pay and allowances until the new pension scheme was introduced. Those pensions were pitifully small. Therefore the personnel who are now pensioned and have to live on those pensions only are in very straitened circumstances. There was no opportunity for the average constable, sergeant, or even inspector, in the old Royal North-West Mounted Police to save any money from their small pay. Therefore I hope when the government does give consideration to this matter, as I feel sure it must now do since it must realize that it is the wish of members on all sides of this house that something be done about this matter at this session, it will also give further consideration to the possibility of including an increase in the pensions of the ex-members of the Royal North-West Mounted Police and of the permanent force of this country.
I do not helieve this house will be satisfied with listening to a lot of figures the Minister of Finance will put on the record later, perhaps only to show that it is going to cost this country a great deal of money. It is not for me to suggest any particular means by which the extra money could be raised. I believe it is readily available. We have a large surplus. All kinds of taxes are being put on. I am not at all sure that I am in favour of the particular method of taxation suggested by the hon. member for Fort William, but let the government decide how it is going to raise the money. As I say, this house will not be satisfied with a whole lot of figures to try to prove it is going to cost the prosperous citizens of this country something to help out the underprivileged, aged, retired servants of this country.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Fort William, on his persistence in focusing our attention on this matter. There is no greater humanitarian anywhere in Canada than the hon. member for Fort William. He is constantly championing the cause of the poor, the weak and the helpless, and it is most appropriate that he should introduce this resolution at this time.
[Mr. Pearkes.l
The hon. member has proposed his resolution in the following words:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants who were retired when salaries were low, so as to bring such pensions more in line with those of the present.
It will be seen that this resolution does not call for a general increase for all civil servants. It is limited to a certain specific group, namely those who were retired when salaries were low. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is a point in its favour, because with this restriction the cost of implementing the resolution will be much lower than would be necessitated by a general increase.
There are many groups of people in Canada, especially in the low income brackets, who are feeling the pinch of inflation, and were it possible we should like to help them all. But to offset the effects of inflation on all low-income groups by direct payments from the federal treasury is simply beyond the financial capacity of Canada even when we take into consideration our rapidly expanding economy. Besides that, for many groups there are other and better ways of helping, but there is no other way of helping the pensioners. Of all the low-income groups, of course, those with fixed incomes feel the pinch of inflation the worst, and no group has a greater claim than the particular group singled out by this resolution, namely the civil servants who retired when salaries were low.
The theory behind pensions is that having given the best years of their lives to the service of their government and their country, the civil servants are entitled to a minimum of security on retirement. This security was held out as an inducement when civil servants were recruited in the past, and it was also used as a justification for paying much lower salaries to civil servants than would be paid by industry and commerce for similar services involving comparable duties and responsibilities. This minimum security is almost in the nature of a contract between the government and the civil servant. A civil servant who has retired has fulfilled his part of the contract both by accepting a lower salary than he could command in industry and also by making his own direct contribution toward that security.
It is very easy to blame inflation on government and government policy. The truth is that we are all to blame. Inflation is mainly the result of the public will. Government spends money sometimes even when perhaps it should not, not because it wants to but because the public demand it. Fixing the blame for inflation is beside

the point. The main point is that inflation is a fact and has been a fact for so many years that many people, even economists, are now inclined to accept it as a normal condition.
Mild inflation even at an almost unnoticeable rate of approximately 2 per cent per year will depreciate the dollar 50 per cent in 25 years. Wage earners have a chance to keep abreast of this depreciation through wage increases which will perhaps give them $2 where 25 years ago they received only $1. Salaried workers also demand and receive salary increases to enable them to keep up with the decline in purchasing power. The poor pensioner with a fixed income, however, is stuck. He has no pressure which he can bring to bear, no bargaining power and no way of protecting himself. His only hope is that this parliament will take some action to protect him from the steady devaluation of our currency, some of which is actually built into our economy.
The civil servant who worked for a low salary in return for security on retirement and who made his contribution toward that security in good faith has a bona fide claim upon the government to provide that security. In fact he has a double claim, because the low salary which he accepted on the assumption of security on retirement prevented him from making his own provision for his later years. On the other hand the size of his pension remains the same while the dollars in which he is paid by way of pension are worth about half as much as the dollars he contributed.
The hon. member for Fort William cited $60 per month as an average pension for retired civil servants. If $60 is the average then it must surely follow that there are many pensioners who are trying to live on much less, and that would certainly include the group envisaged by this resolution. In my own riding there are several retired civil servants who are living on much less than even $50 per month. It must be remembered that the civil servant's pension is not for himself alone. It is not meant as a subsistence for himself alone but for his family as well, and in most cases two people have to live on the small pension. In many cases this pension which has been earned is less than the amount received in old age assistance or even the amount paid to old age pensioners. It must be remembered too that old age pensioners have no means of supplementing their income. At their age they are off the labour market; nobody wants them, and instead of giving them employment we require their jobs to take care of the increase in the labour force.
Pensions
Personally I believe that the retirement age of 65 is too low. When a person reaches the age of 65 and is in sound health I think it would be better if retirement were made optional instead of compulsory. A noticeable difference exists between a person who reaches the age of 65 today and those who attained that age 20 years ago. Our improvements in health standards have not only prolonged man's life but have prolonged his vitality, his energy and his ability to produce. It seems that in a country like Canada, especially in an expanding economy where labour may become scarce, it is not in the best interests of the country to fail to make use of the productive capacity of people over 65 years of age.
For the reasons I have outlined, Mr. Speaker, namely that the employment of civil servants involves conditions which are somewhat in the nature of a contract, conditions which they on their part fulfilled by working for lower salaries than could be obtained in comparable jobs in industry and also by paying contributions in dollars the purchasing power of which was far in excess of that of the dollars in which their pensions are paid, I believe the government has a special responsibility to this particular group. It is a matter not only of justice but of honour that their pensions should be increased to bring them in line with the purchasing power they represented at the date of retirement. For that reason it gives me much pleasure to support the resolution.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Lethbridge said when he was speaking, we in this corner are going to support this resolution, and along with others who have spoken I would like to commend the venerable and honourable member for Fort William for having given us the opportunity to say a few words about this very important matter.
I listened quite attentively to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South. The one thing he tried to stress quite strongly, Mr. Speaker, was that the government had a moral responsibility; I think that is putting it quite mildly. Yet he claimed that the fall in the value of the dollar so far as purchasing power is concerned was not the fault of the present government. Well, I am going to make the statement-it is not within the terms of this resolution to enlarge upon it, even if there were time-that since 1939 we have had fiscal and financial policies in this country which have reduced the purchasing power of the dollar by at least 47 per cent. And I maintain that the government, by wise leadership and by different financial

Pensions
and fiscal policies, could have altered that trend and made it a different situation.
It is perfectly all right to say that the government is not at fault, but the financial leaders, and those who set policies in this country are certainly at fault when they allow these things to run rampant; and the end is not yet in sight. We believe, and there is every reason to believe, that the cost of living will continue to rise in this country during the coming year. Some people speak of it as creeping inflation, though the word "inflation" is, I am sure, improperly used. Nevertheless we will borrow the term and go along with it. It is said that the price rise will continue throughout the coming year, and I am quite satisfied that this will be due in no small measure to the high interest rates and the credit restriction policies which can definitely be laid at the door of this government.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo-I do not know what he was trying to prove- was telling us about people in his riding who were living on $50 and less per month. When he used that word "living" he should have used the word "existing".
As I read through this resolution, I see it begins, "That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability-" and so on. I expect one of the members of this government will rise in his place and say, as we have been told on many occasions, that the government is always considering matters which will be of benefit to the people of this country who are living on low incomes. But I am going to tell this hon. gentleman before he rises that this problem can be killed by consideration, because if it takes them long enough to consider it then those who should be benefiting will be under the ground. I hope that will not be the kind of consideration they will receive and the kind of answer we will get from this government.
The resolution calls for an increase in pensions and, of course, that naturally means giving out more dollars. It has been pointed out that in large measure, at least, the trouble is due to the fact that the dollar today has not the purchasing power it had when these pensions were fixed 20 years ago, when a person could live on $50 or $60. Of course that is not the case today. Industry has become aware of that fact, and there are many plants across the country where wages to employees are tied to the cost of living and rise as may be necessary to support them in the standard of living to which they are entitled by the wage scale or by the power of their earnings. So it is not asking too much if we request that this government should consider these employees who have

given the best years of their lives to the service of the state, and who are existing today on a standard of living which is certainly not a just reward for all the years they have given to this country.
I shall refer, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich did, to the mounted police. I happen to have a very personal friend in that category who retired from the service some years ago on a pension of less than $35 a month. I think many of us who happen to have been homesteaders on the prairies, or pioneers in any part of this country, will remember with a great deal of satisfaction the efforts of those redcoats as they policed the pioneer regions. At that time, Mr. Speaker, their wages were certainly not high. It was impossible for them to save any money from their meagre earnings; yet when they reached the age when they were of no further use to their employers they were expected to live on a pension of $35 per month or less.
This friend of mine is certainly in a difficult situation. He has a wife who was stricken with paralysis, so you can imagine the conditions in which they are trying to live. He came to me a couple of years ago and asked if I could do something for him. You know, these old members of the police force have a pride which tends to prevent them asking for what is looked upon as relief. Of course these days we have a different word; we call it welfare. But, anyhow, he did not want to stoop so low, as he put it, as to ask for welfare, and an effort was made to see if there was any possibility of having the pension increased. Of course that was impossible, and the only advice I could give him was that he should swallow his pride and make application to the British Columbia government for welfare payments, which he did, and as a result his troubles were alleviated to some extent. But that means getting help in a way which is not in accordance with what should be the high ideals of the Canadian government as the employer of these people.
So we must recognize that, as this resolution asks, pensions should be increased. Of course another way this could be done would be to decrease the prices of the goods they have to buy. I do not think we want to see such drastic action at the present time. It would upset our economy too much. But whether we give them extra dollars, whether we give them certificates for food, or in what manner we try to solve the problem, the main thing is that we must bring their pensions up to a proper ratio with the prices of the goods they need to sustain life.

I have great pleasure in doing all I can to encourage the government to give consideration to the matter, and by that I mean immediate consideration, not consideration that will carry on until these people have passed to the great beyond. Let the government give immediate consideration and see that justice is done to these people, and that they are given pensions in keeping with the services they have rendered to the country.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall only say a tew words in order that other hon. members may have an opportunity to speak. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Fort William on having raised this matter. It is not a new question. On many occasions I have had the opportunity to say something about civil servants retired on small pensions, especially those retired on pensions based on the salaries that existed some 10 or 15 years ago.
As I have said before, the civil service of Canada is the best in the world, and because our civil servants are the best they are entitled to the best treatment. I have also said before, and I am not afraid to repeat it, that the government should be the best employer. Although the superannuation act is very good and has been amended often to make it better still, I do not agree that we should base payments of pensions to civil servants entirely upon the contract. I think the government has a duty exceeding the bounds of an ordinary contract; and when its employees, who are human beings, have served their country during the best years of their lives and now find themselves in a position of need, it is up to us in parliament to raise our voices and give the necessary support to any legislation which will improve the standard of living of retired civil servants and place it on the same level as that of those who are now retiring on pensions based on present salaries.
I quite agree that it might be said that the resolution is a bit vague. If we were to accept the resolution as it stands it would no doubt mean a little more than some of us have in mind, because the resolution states in part, "to increase the pensions of civil servants who were retired when salaries were low." Of course that is relative, and I suppose all salaries were low then compared with what they are today. As the resolution is worded it would apply to those who retired some years ago when they were receiving salaries of $5,000 or $6,000 a year, whereas persons in similar positions today are getting $10,000 or $11,000. I am sure the hon. member for Fort William had in mind those who were retired on pensions based on low incomes compared with the present incomes of similar grades in the civil service. Such pensions do not afford
Pensions
a scale of living comparable to that of persons in similar positions retiring today.
As one who has lived in Ottawa all his life I am most anxious that something should be done in the direction indicated in the resolution. I recall too well the hundreds and hundreds of people in the city of Ottawa with only 10 or 15 years of employment who were let out on the streets during the depression of the early thirties with very low pensions, and who by the time of the prosperity brought about by the war were too old to seek further employment. They were left with the pensions handed out to them in the early thirties.
I do not want that situation to occur again, and I do not think it will because at present the salaries of civil servants have been geared much closer to the cost of living index. Nevertheless I am particularly in favour of the resolution if it means, as I see it, that it affects a certain group of people who have already been retired and whose pensions have been based on salaries which were lower than those existing at present in the civil service.
I do not think it is asking too much to ask that parliament should take action immediately. It is not as if it were going to be a continuing vote for many years to come. I think a calculation could be made very easily as to what amount of money would be required, because only a certain existing group of people are affected, and whatever the amount of the vote it would be fixed. The same situation would not occur each year. The amount would diminish every year, and I think it could be easily calculated by the Department of Finance.
As I have said before, I have great sympathy for those who have pensions of $5,000, $4,000 or $3,500, but I believe it would be much better if any sums of money parliament might vote following such a resolution were spent on alleviating the circumstances of those who are really in need, who only have very low pensions based on low incomes while employed in the civil service. I do not think it was the intention of the mover of the resolution to increase the incomes of those who are in comfortable circumstances.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, that I readily agree with the resolution, because I think the mover has in mind all the things I have said. I hope that the government will give the matter its immediate attention.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the resolution. I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa East, who has just taken his seat, that salaries and pensions should be related to the cost

Pensions
of living. I think that is the whole difficulty as far as this matter is concerned. I am pleased that the hon. member for Fort William has brought it to the attention of the house. I think most hon. members would have felt much better if the government had brought in a resolution to amend the superannuation act. That would seem more practical, because frankly I know that most of us in the house realize what private members' resolutions mean. They are simply brought in here and nothing practical is ever done about them.
This is a subject which requires the attention of the house; and unless the resolution is passed, unless the government takes action, nothing will be done this year just as nothing has been done in previous years. Having listened to the debate today, I am not going to repeat the many arguments that have been advanced because this is a subject that really speaks for itself.	>
As a matter of fact there is no necessity for a debate in this house at all. If you go anywhere across this country you will find that a great injustice is being done to the class of people mentioned in the resolution. It is a very hard and difficult world for those people who are trying to live on pensions and superannuation allowances which are practically 50 per cent of what they should be. They are based on the value of money 15, 20 and 25 years ago and on the cost of living at that time. They should be brought up to date.
Hon. members have mentioned the fact that this country of ours has expanded a great deal in the last 15 or 20 years. I suppose we are one of the wealthiest countries in the world. I suppose we have the greatest natural resources of almost any country in the world. From those natural resources and from the energy of our people we have an abundance, and there is prosperity. There is no question about that fact. There could not help but be prosperity in a country such as this. All people in all walks of life should share in that prosperity.
Our superannuated civil servants should share in that prosperity just the same as everyone else. When they have reached an age when it is impossible for them to do it otherwise, having given the service to the country years previously and having to a great extent laid the foundation for the prosperity we are now enjoying, they should be given this consideration and should have an opportunity to share in this prosperity.
If I may I should like to read an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star just before the new year in speaking of this and kindred subjects. This editorial states:
The answer is that not all Canadians share our national abundance.

That is very true. Not all Canadians share our national abundance. The editorial continues:
A sad contradiction in our prosperity is the fact that good times mean not a higher, but a lower standard of living for many. Surely, in a land of plenty, in a country teeming with prosperity, our senior citizens, our recipients of mothers' allowances and others dependent on government pensions, should get more consideration. In the new year, let us resolve to find new ways of sharing our country's bounty by attending to these and similar problems. In this way we can transform "prosperity" from a national slogan to a real and meaningful way of life for all Canadians.
That is what would happen to many people if this resolution which has been brought in by the hon. member for Fort William had been brought in by the government and an amendment were being considered by the government at the present time. We all know that day after day and week after week prices keep going up, wages keep going up, the cost of living keeps going up, and the condition of these people keeps getting worse and worse. They are placed in an almost impossible position.
I should like to be in a position to say a few words with regard to veterans pensions, but I know I would be out of order in doing so. However, this is another class of people in this country who are not enjoying the prosperity of the country which all are entitled to enjoy. Just by way of comparison may I point out that last year, in 1956, the pension of a veteran was $1,500; for a soldier it was $1,932 and for a civil service cleaner, $2,760.
We all know that the soldier's pension was supposed to be based on the corresponding pay received by a worker in ordinary labour but the worker received $2,760, the pensioner $1,500.
There are many more things I should like to say, but most of them have been mentioned here tonight. The hon. member for Vancouver South spoke about government private members' resolutions. He said they should be considered on their merit, that is that we should have an open vote in the house. I have always felt that there is on the house a moral obligation to support matters of this kind which are brought up by private members.
I should like to say to the government members of this house that they have many opportunities which we in the opposition do not have. I am sometimes rather surprised. The only way we in the opposition can bring matters to the attention of the government and of the house is by means of a resolution. The hon. member who has brought in this resolution has the ear of the cabinet. Time and time again I have heard him in this house say that everything

was right with this world, that the government was in power, God is in his heaven and nothing they do can be wrong. The hon. member can consult with the cabinet. He can consult with his fellow members. He can bring this matter up in his caucus.
I should like to ask him here tonight how many times he has brought this matter before the cabinet and the other members of his party to see if he could not influence them in caucus and influence his cabinet to have this done. I sometimes think that unless a government member has done those things, unless he has exhausted every opportunity he has with his own people-before bringing a resolution before the house, it savours somewhat of hypocrisy.

speechtext:
I do not know how to please the members on the other side of the house. They have the opportunity to speak at their ease as they wish. Again I am going to tell those hon. members that I am going to speak any time I feel like it, especially in order to support such a good measure as the one which has been presented in this house today.
In addition, I will assure my colleagues on the other side that the government must be well aware of the wishes of this house in so far as the acceptance of this motion is concerned. I think we have the consensus of members here indicating they are in favour of this motion which is brought forward at this time and which is absolutely justified. At the same time I am going to say again that members on this side ought to be able to rise without hearing complaints from members on the other side when we feel it is time to speak.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to continue my remarks in French and to say, as I was saying a moment ago in a tongue which is not my own and which I use only with some difficulty, that I will take every opportunity to avail myself of the privilege of raising my voice in this house especially when the point at issue is the endorsement of a proposal as fair as the one which is now under discussion.
I am not surprised to find the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) introducing this resolution. For many years now I have had the opportunity to see how solicitous he is towards the less fortunate. I know with what devotion he has served, not only his constituents, but all those who have come to him for help. I therefore repeat that, coming from the hon. member for Fort William,' this proposal does not surprise me in the least. I may add that it is particularly timely, coming as it does on the eve of the budget for the fiscal year 1957-1958.
Moreover, I am convinced that this resolution will be taken into serious consideration by this government which, on all occasions, has lent a helping hand to those classes which directly or indirectly are dependent on it. Nor must it be forgotten that this government has been the great champion of the social measures enjoyed by the people of Canada.

Pensions
Let me suggest that it might also be advisable to consider allowing public servants to stay in office beyond the age of 65. They should be given the opportunity, the advantage, the freedom to decide for themselves whether or not they will keep on working beyond age 65, although there should be a limit set at 70.
Today, on reaching 70, people have not aged as much as in the past. Statistics prove that the span of life is longer today. Today's worker seems to be stronger or at least more resistant. Could it be that less strain is imposed upon him? I doubt it. At any rate, everyone agrees that today a man of 70 has aged less than was the case 30 or 40 years ago. Obviously, I am not talking about myself, who even remarried a short time ago, but of those who are familiar with statistics. They will certainly admit that I am right in saying that it is easier today for a man to work until he is 70 than it used to be for a man of the same age.
It is necessary, Mr. Speaker, to consider carefully the condition of the man who retired on a pension, say in 1939 or 1940. He had figured on a standard of living based on the value of the dollar at the time of his retirement. But what is the value today of a pension of let us say, $75 a month, when we think of how much our dollar has depreciated during those 17 years?
I am in favour of this measure for, after all-i do not know if I have the right word to express what I mean-I consider a pension as a retirement salary. A retirement salary is one on which the retired person must count to provide for his own needs and those of his dependents, if he has any. If everybody agrees that a pension is a retirement salary, we should therefore, in the case of pensioned people, consider the salary increase granted to workers who are still employed either in the civil service or in private industry. We should also take into account the difference in salaries between 1940 and 1957, and establish a pension with a proportional rate as high in 1957 as it was in 1939.
There is no shadow of a doubt that the problem facing those who depend solely on their pension is a serious one, and the mover of the present resolution is to be commended, for it is indeed pitiable to find that civil servants who have given the best years of their life to their country are often left in a worse position than their fellow workers employed by private enterprise, as I am told that some private industries have agreed of their own accord to grant a raise in pension

to those who have retired 15, or 20, or even only 10 years ago.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I only hope they won't accuse me of-

I am going to take my seat before ten o'clock so hon. members cannot accuse me of talking out this resolution. I am not going to ask for the adjournment of the debate. I only wish to underline to my colleagues the fact that I have the right to express myself. I am not going to talk out this motion; I am going to follow the good example given by those who have spoken on this question, and I hope the government will consider what has been said here and that the resolution will be not only taken into consideration by them but that the objective will be put into practice.

I think it is obvious that this is an expenditure which would not be inflationary, but which would be economically sound and politically popular.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra for placing on the record this afternoon certain of my questions that were answered by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. I am not going to read them; I merely wish to draw attention to the fact that the highest paid pension under the Public Service Superannuation Act is $875 a month, or $10,500 a year. That would appear to me quite an ample pension but, Mr. Speaker, I draw your attention to the fact that there are 5,644 of our fellow Canadians who gave their very best service to this country many years ago, when it was anticipated that the superannuation allowance would be adequate, who are now in the unfortunate position of getting $21.03 a month. I am sure there is no member in this house who thinks of that figure with any pride. It amounts to around 70 cents a day.
The last time I visited the penitentiary some years ago they told me it costs the tax-

payers about $6 a day to keep those who are in such institutions. It is hard tor me to understand that our economy should require upwards of $6 a day to keep people in institutions while we expect our superannuated civil servants should be able to get by on as low as $21.03 a month. I am indebted to the provincial secretary of the British Columbia superannuated civil servants' organization for a letter he sent to all members in February, 1954. At that time he pointed out:
For five long years we have repeatedly drawn the attention of parliament-without result or acknowledgment-to the present-day problems of many retired federal civil servants, from coast to coast, and surely it is not too soon to expect that appropriate action will now be taken to deal with this question, by granting to all those receiving less than $150 per month, a bonus graded accordingly, as conditions warrant.
This afternoon my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre drew our attention to the fact that years ago Great Britain and the United States recognized that retired civil servants are not able to go into the labour market and compete with the younger people and take advantage of the prosperity that younger people now talk about. They are the victims of the fact that the dollar they expected to have is now worth 50 cents.
In the United States, under Bill S2968, superannuated civil servants who were getting $1,000 a year were increased to $1,250 in 1948, and later to $1,562.50. In Great Britain on a number of occasions substantial increases have been granted, and I understand that our province of Saskatchewan is the only province in Canada that has made provision for additional bonus payments to civil servants who are on pension and find it impossible to meet the high cost of living with that inadequate pension. I hope the Minister of Finance will accept the proposals made from all sections of the house.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO INCREASE PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with everyone else who has given his nod of approval to the hon. member for Fort William for bringing the motion before the house. In saying that, I think the house will permit me also to say that we have found the hon. member prompted by sympathy and warm-heartedness for a great many people, and I am sure the sympathy and warm-heartedness which are part of his character and nature prompt him to assist people who he feels are living on inadequate pensions.
I go ahead, of course, at once to say that others in this house, before today and tonight, have joined in that approach to this question, and have moved the house and the government on other occasions to give con-
Pensions
sideration to the retired civil servants and the pensions which are being paid to them.
Unfortunately the Minister of Finance is in a position where he must try to determine whether or not the sympathy is not only just sympathy for people whose income is low, but also whether he ought to consider that it would be justified to expend public moneys in increasing the pensions and, if so, the terms on which the increase should be granted and the principle which should be involved in making the increase, together with any other decisions which might logically follow from such a change.
I wish to go back, if I may, to some of the remarks which were made during the afternoon and the evening, and in particular to the reference which has been made that this debate has gone on at least for 10 years in the House of Commons. It seems to me that if this were so-and I presume it is so-there must have been a reasonably good case made for not doing anything in the meantime, because it seems to me that a case which cannot change the mind of the government during that time may have certain difficulties attendant upon it which may be quite as important as the original case itself.
I have listened tonight to the arguments in favour of the resolution, and I want to go over some of them to test them to see if they are valid, and to see in the end what we have left by way of suggestions and proposals which might be made to meet the plight of these people.
Now, the first, the obvious and I think the continuing claim on behalf of those people is that the cost of living has increased since they obtained their pensions, and therefore allowance ought to be made for that by the government by way of increasing the pension. May I point out that while I recognize that the cost of living looms large in the thinking of those who have to maintain a household, and looms large in the minds of many people who look upon it as an easy index to use in any demands for wage increases, or pension increases, or any form of increase in income, it is hardly the final word on any subject; and in particular it is hardly the final word which the government could use in altering the expenditures made out of public moneys because of the very insecurity of the index and the constant change in it.
Hon. members ought to recall that in that 10-year period, if I am correct, we had a decline in the consumer price index, if I may use that term, from I think about 1947, which was the first date mentioned tonight, until 1949 or probably 1950. We had a substantial increase in the consumer price index during 1950, 1951 and 1952. Then I think we had a levelling off, if not a slight decline, until

Pensions
June or July of last year, and an increase since that time. I am speaking without notes, of course, but it does seem to me that for the 10-year period I have described accurately enough for our purposes the alterations in the consumer price index.
If it were the case that the government would be expected to alter its wage payments and its pension payments-based on the cost of living index, I shall say for the moment, alone-you would see there would be hardly a session of parliament when we would not be altering these to some degree. You would see as well, sir, that the civil service associations, having regard to their wage levels would hardly expect us to use this index when it went down; and I for one would not think they would not have a good case in making the objection, because one should have a continuity of employment and wage level with an increase based not only on terms of service and ability and the like but we would hope a steadily increasing wage level from year to year or at least, if the conditions were justified, from time to time.
On that basis, then, I suggest that while the consumer price index might be a suitable handle to use to argue any given case, it is not by any means too reliable nor should it be considered any more than a portion of any argument about wages or pension levels.
The second point I wish to make-and this is one which everyone who has spoken today has either overlooked or has passed by with only a passing reference-is the very large number of these people whose income by way of pension is low because of their short term of service in the civil service. Mention has been made of this by some speakers. I must confess that I am not able to present to the house the number out of the 13,000-odd we are talking about who had service of less than say 10 years. It is my fault that I have not been able to get the figures for this occasion, but as I think I pointed out on another occasion, Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons hon. members have by way of argument in this case is the number of low pensions paid in Canada. I think almost without exception every speaker has not gone on in fairness to say why we have such a large number of low pensions and superannuation payments for civil servants.
The reason, as everyone who has looked at this question knows, is that Canada pays superannuation earlier than any other country that has been mentioned here tonight; so that by our very generosity-although it is not generosity, I think it is a very wise program -by the very fact that we give to civil servants an advantage not obtained in either

the civil service of the United Kingdom or that of the United States, we find that our records indicate low pensions to a great many who otherwise would not receive pensions. To that extent, then, hon. members are inclined to say we are not being fair with these people in paying them such low amounts.
The motion itself speaks of increasing pensions for those who were retired when salaries were low. I must apologize for not being in the house when the hon. member for Fort William began his remarks, though I came in as soon as I could. I do not know whether he defined what he meant by way of time or what he meant by way of a cut-off date. If you go back 30 years, of course, you will find pensions were low because they were in proportion to the income at that time, and the longer a person lives after retirement the more likely it is that there will be a greater disparity between the pension he is receiving and that which he would receive if he had retired the day before. That of course is obvious; but I am going to assume that the reference here is to pensions which were established shall I say before the war for the sake of argument.
The purpose of a pension is to provide a retiring allowance based on the income, length of service and the like, and is fixed with relation to a definite amount. That is, we have not a system whereby one can alter his pension of his own volition. It has been argued today by several hon. members that because the value of money has declined noticeably, especially for those who were retired a number of years ago, in some manner the government is responsible for this and therefore ought to accept the burden of righting the so-called injustice by making an increased payment.
I would not want that argument to pass without some answer; but I do want to say at this point, sir, that all my arguments are directed to seeing if this case has in fact a good basis other than one of natural sympathy for people who are not perhaps receiving by way of income what is required at the moment, just simply to see in the first place if there is any logical action that might be taken which would not lead us into other disparities quite as bad as the present with which we would have to deal.
The argument that the government is responsible for inflation and therefore ought to pay pensions based on present-day costs rather than costs at the time of retirement is based, I think, on the quotation cited by the hon.

member for Winnipeg North Centre in which he says, quoting Mr. Pethick-'Lawrence:
. . . at some future date there is an assumption, unwritten and unspecified, but nevertheless implied. That is the stability of the purchasing power of money.
Except for those contracts, Mr. Speaker, calling for the payment of the amount of the debt in gold I do not know of any such principle in any commercial transaction, and I have not seen any in my time. You will recall that I interrupted my hon. friend to ask if he agreed with that.
